subject: physics
question_text: Explain conduction, convection and radiation with examples.

verification.note: Asked in TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, March 2016 (Q18), March 2020 (Q18) and March 2025 (Q17) — Section B, 4 marks each time. The four-way split, one mark for each method and one for the comparison, is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced from those papers. Physics hand-checked: conduction and convection need a material medium, radiation does not and travels at the speed of light; in conduction the particles stay in place, in convection the heated material itself moves.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Conduction
lines: Conduction is the transfer of heat through
a body from its hotter part to its colder
part, without the material itself moving.
The particles vibrate more strongly and
pass energy to their neighbours.
Example: the free end of a metal spoon
kept in hot water becomes warm.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The definition and one example together earn it.
steps.why: In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions, so the only way they can move energy along is by vibrating against their neighbours.
common_mistakes: Saying the hot particles travel along the rod. In conduction the particles stay in place and only the energy moves.

recall.must_convey: That conduction moves heat through a body without the material moving, as in a metal spoon in hot water.
accept: heat passes without the material moving

steps.memory_tip: Conduction: the energy moves, the material does not. A metal spoon in hot water.

steps.label: Convection
lines: Convection is the transfer of heat by the
actual movement of the heated material.
A heated liquid or gas becomes less dense
and rises, and colder material comes down
to take its place.
Example: water heated at the bottom of a
vessel, and the land and sea breezes.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Say that the heated material itself moves.
steps.why: A liquid or a gas can flow, so the heated portion carries its energy away with it. A solid cannot flow, which is why convection does not occur in solids.
common_mistakes: Saying convection occurs in solids. A solid cannot flow, so the heated material cannot rise.

recall.must_convey: That in convection the heated liquid or gas itself rises and carries the heat, as in water heated at the bottom.

steps.memory_tip: Convection: the hot material itself rises. It works in liquids and gases only.

steps.label: Radiation
lines: Radiation is the transfer of heat by
electromagnetic waves. It needs no
material medium and travels at the speed
of light.
Example: the heat received from the Sun
across empty space.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Write that no medium is needed.
steps.why: Electromagnetic waves carry energy by themselves, so no particles are needed to pass it along. That is why the heat of the Sun crosses the vacuum of space.
common_mistakes: Saying radiation needs air to travel. It travels through vacuum.

recall.must_convey: That radiation carries heat by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium, as in the heat from the Sun.

steps.memory_tip: Only radiation crosses a vacuum — that is how the heat of the Sun reaches us.

steps.label: How the three differ
lines: Conduction and convection need a material
medium; radiation does not.
In conduction the particles stay in place;
in convection they move with the heat.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. One line separating the three methods earns it.
steps.why: The three methods differ in what carries the energy — vibrating particles, moving material, or waves. Naming the carrier is what tells them apart.
common_mistakes: Writing three definitions with no line comparing them. The comparison is a separate mark.

recall.must_convey: That conduction and convection need a medium while radiation does not.
accept: the first two need a medium

steps.memory_tip: Vibration, flow, waves. Only the waves cross empty space.

insider_note: Three definitions and three examples, one mark each — a definition written without its example rarely holds the full mark.
